newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Canberra to hammer out finances with states.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canberra to hammer out finances with states.

text.p: Australian federal and state governments will hammer out their fiscal arrangements on Friday at the annual annual Premiers Conference and Loans Council meetings.
The federal government's plans for the conference have not been detailed, but really big cuts in the federal grants to the states are not expected.

The grants were cut last year, and Treasurer Peter Costello has said that although the federal government needs to find more budget savings this year it will generally leave alone the areas that suffered last year.

Moreover, the states said last year they were making a once-and-for-all contribution to the federal government's fiscal repair programme when they sacrificed funding with a recurrent value of about A$700 million a year.

A federal source said Prime Minister John Howard will also pursue other matters requiring federal-state co-ordination at the gathering -- native title, small business deregulation, the housing policy and health policy.
In all of those areas the federal government has or is developing a policy but the states retain constitutional power.
Howard and the state premiers will meet over dinner on Thursday to discuss those issues, of which native title is by far the dominant.

The meeting is not, however, expected to make any final decision on how to deal with the High Court's recent extension of native title to leasehold crown land, part of its judgement in the Wik case in December.
"Howard will not have a final position to detail on Wik," said one federal official.
The Premiers Conference is a regular event in Australian politics because the states gave up their power to impose income taxes during World War Two.
Since then, they have relied on federal funding -- effectively, their share of federal income tax -- in the form of so-called grants.
The two sides meet at the Premiers Conference to agree on the value of the grants before their budgets and on the same day hold a formal meeting to co-ordinate public borrowing -- the Loans Council.
There are two main types of federal grants to the states -- specific purpose and general.
State officials see the general grants as particularly secure against further cuts this year because of the way they were cut last year.
In the 1996 Premiers Conference the general grants -- which states can spend as they please -- were cut heavily but temporarily.
They lost large lumps in the three fiscal years to 1998/99 (July-June) after which they were scheduled to return to their previously planned levels.
One state financial official said that raised the stakes in further short-term cuts, because the states had already sacrificed so much in that period.
Long-term cuts were more politically viable, but fiscally unimportant to a federal government trying to balance its budget by 1998/99, he said.
Specific-purpose grants have to be spent on the functions determined by the federal government -- for example, hospitals.
These grants, cut by about A$500 million last year, were more vulnerable, the official said.
